headings.title: Introduction to the Misoprostol-Only Regimen
headings.content: The misoprostol-only medical protocol offers a safe, highly effective method for pregnancy termination, especially in low-resource settings where mifepristone remains unavailable or restricted. Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue initially developed to prevent gastric ulcers caused by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Over decades of global clinical use, healthcare providers recognized its potent uterotonic properties, leading to its widespread adoption in reproductive health care. Unlike combination regimens that require both mifepristone and misoprostol, the standalone protocol relies entirely on repeated doses of misoprostol to soften the cervix and stimulate myometrial contractions. This makes medical abortion accessible in primary healthcare clinics across Nigeria, empowering nurses and midwives to provide timely, life-saving care within their legal and professional scopes.

headings.title: Mechanism of Action and Pharmacology
headings.content: Misoprostol acts directly on the myometrium and the cervix to induce abortion. When absorbed into the bloodstream, it binds to specific prostaglandin receptors on uterine smooth muscle cells, triggering intracellular calcium release and powerful, rhythmic contractions. Simultaneously, it alters the collagen matrix of the cervix, causing cervical softening, effacement, and dilatation. Pharmacokinetically, misoprostol is rapidly absorbed after oral, sublingual, vaginal, or buccal administration. Sublingual and buccal routes yield the highest peak plasma concentrations and greatest systemic bioavailability, whereas vaginal administration provides a more sustained, gradual release with fewer systemic side effects such as shivering and fever. Hepatic metabolism breaks the drug down into its active metabolite, misoprostol acid, which is then excreted primarily through the kidneys.

headings.title: Clinical Indications and Eligibility Criteria
headings.content:
A thorough clinical evaluation must precede any misoprostol-only protocol to confirm eligibility and rule out contraindications. The regimen is indicated for medical termination of intrauterine pregnancies up to the gestational limit supported by local guidelines, as well as for the management of early pregnancy loss, such as missed or incomplete miscarriages. 

- **Gestational age confirmation**: Accurate dating via ultrasound or reliable last menstrual period is mandatory.
- **Ectopic pregnancy exclusion**: The drug is completely ineffective and dangerous if an extrauterine pregnancy is present.
- **IUD removal**: Any intrauterine contraceptive device must be removed prior to initiating treatment.
- **Absence of allergy**: Patients with a known hypersensitivity to prostaglandins must not receive the medication.
- **Coagulopathy check**: Severe bleeding disorders or concurrent anticoagulant therapy rule out the outpatient use of standalone misoprostol.

headings.title: Standard Dosage and Administration Routes
headings.content:
The efficacy of a misoprostol-only regimen depends heavily on correct dosing intervals and routes. Because a single dose often yields lower complete abortion rates than combination therapy, repeated dosing schedules are standard practice. 

| Route | Typical Dose | Interval | Clinical Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sublingual | 800 mcg | Every 3 hours | Higher systemic side effects |
| Vaginal | 800 mcg | Every 3 to 12 hours | Requires deep insertion; less shivering |
| Buccal | 800 mcg | Every 3 hours | Dissolve in cheeks for 30 minutes |

Nurses must ensure tablets are held in the mouth or moistened properly if vaginal dry tablets are used. Adherence to the prescribed timing ensures optimal uterine activity and minimizes incomplete expulsion.

headings.title: Pre-Procedure Assessment and Counseling
headings.content: Pre-procedure preparation establishes a safe clinical environment and ensures the patient is psychologically and physically ready. The nurse must conduct a private, non-judgmental history-taking session to assess gestational age, medical history, and emotional state. Physical assessment includes checking baseline vital signs and performing a bimanual pelvic examination when indicated. Counseling covers what physical sensations to expect, the timeline of bleeding, and the recognition of red-flag symptoms. The nurse must also verify that the patient has a reliable support system at home and access to emergency transport, transforming clinical instructions into actionable, understandable guidance.

headings.title: Expected Side Effects and Normal Process
headings.content: Once misoprostol takes effect, the physiological process mimics a spontaneous miscarriage. The patient will experience moderate to severe uterine cramping, which is a necessary sign that the muscle is working to expel the pregnancy tissue. Vaginal bleeding typically starts within hours of the first dose, often heavier than a normal menstrual period, and may include blood clots or visible gestational tissue. Systemic side effects are temporary and directly related to prostaglandin action; they include transient low-grade fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and headache. Nurses should reassure clients that these symptoms usually subside within 24 hours of completing the medication schedule without requiring specific medical intervention beyond simple analgesics like paracetamol or ibuprofen.

headings.title: Complications and Warning Signs
headings.content: Although generally safe, misoprostol-only regimens carry risks that require immediate medical attention. Excessive bleeding is the most common serious complication, defined clinically as soaking through two large sanitary pads per hour for two consecutive hours. Persistent heavy bleeding can lead to profound anemia or hypovolemic shock. Other red flags include signs of severe systemic infection, such as a high fever lasting beyond 24 hours post-administration, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, or severe pelvic pain that does not improve with standard pain relief. Nurses must instruct patients on exact emergency contact procedures and ensure prompt referral for surgical evacuation if an incomplete abortion or hemorrhage occurs.

headings.title: Post-Abortion Follow-Up and Contraception
headings.content: Comprehensive post-abortion care involves confirming complete evacuation of the uterus and initiating immediate contraception if desired. Ovulation can return as early as two weeks after a medical abortion, meaning a patient can become pregnant before their next menstrual period. Follow-up can be managed through clinical assessment, low-sensitivity urine pregnancy tests, or telephonic check-ins depending on protocol. The nurse plays a pivotal role in contraceptive counseling, offering a wide range of options including injectables, implants, oral contraceptive pills, and intrauterine devices. Providing these methods on the day of treatment or shortly after prevents rapid unplanned repeat pregnancies and supports long-term reproductive health goals.
